help.adaptive.bigrams:
Drilling the letter pairs that trip you up

Not everything that slows you down is a single key. Often it's the hand-off between two — an awkward pair like ‘ny’, ‘rl’ or ‘br’ where your fingers have to travel or cross over. KeyLearn keeps an eye on the pairings where you consistently stumble and weaves more of them into the words it builds for you, so you smooth out the transitions themselves, not just the individual letters on either side.
help.adaptive.confidence:
Confidence that watches accuracy, not just speed

The core signal for how well you know a key has always been how fast you type it. KeyLearn now adds a second opinion drawn from learning science — a technique called Bayesian Knowledge Tracing — that also weighs how cleanly you hit that key. It forgives the occasional slip on a key you clearly know, and it refuses to be fooled by a lucky fast-but-sloppy tap. The two views are blended together, with raw speed still leading by two-to-one, so a letter only counts as mastered when you're both quick and accurate. It's tuned to unlock the next letter at the same comfortable pace you're used to — usually a couple of clean passes — just with a sharper eye on mistakes.
help.adaptive.decay:
Letters quietly fade if you leave them alone

Skills rust when they go unused, and KeyLearn reflects that honestly. A key you haven't practiced in a long time slowly loses a little confidence over real time, so you might see an old letter drift back from green toward red on its own. That's not you getting worse — it's the app gently flagging that the letter is due for a refresh before it truly slips. Your best-ever result for a key is never wiped out; only the current reading softens.
help.adaptive.intro:
The smart layers working behind the scenes

The letter-by-letter cycle above is the backbone of your practice, but KeyLearn runs a few extra adaptive helpers on top of it. You never switch these on or think about them — they quietly shape every session so your time lands where it pays off most. Here's what each one is doing while you type.
help.adaptive.review:
A quick warm-up on the keys you're due to review

Letters you picked up a while ago but haven't touched in a few sessions get surfaced first, as a short warm-up at the start of your practice. It works the way a good flashcard deck resurfaces a card right before you'd forget it: reviewing a skill at that fading edge is exactly what pushes it into long-term memory. So don't be surprised to revisit an old friend before meeting anyone new.
help.example1: Example 1 went from 30 to 70 WPM over 15 days, with 4 hours 20 minutes of total practice — the accuracy-aware confidence blend kept steering each session toward the keys that were genuinely holding them back.
help.example2: Example 2 climbed from 35 to 70 WPM over 12 days, with just 2 hours and 20 minutes of practice — the spaced-review warm-up meant less time was needed to make each gain stick.
help.example3: Example 3 made a solid leap from under 20 to 40 WPM over 11 days, with 5 hours and 30 minutes of practice — the bigram drills smoothing out the awkward letter pairs that had been the real bottleneck.
help.example4: Example 4 held steady at roughly 70 WPM (already quite fast) across 11 days and 2 hours 10 minutes of practice, while accuracy kept climbing — the BKT blend only marks a key mastered once it's both fast and clean, so the extra reps went straight into fewer mistakes.
help.example5: Example 5 improved from 20 to 45 WPM over 22 days and about 10 hours of practice (progress isn't always fast, and that's okay) — and whenever older letters faded, the decay nudges surfaced them again for a quick refresh before they slipped for real.

help.rule1.body: The very first time you practice, KeyLearn has no data on your skills yet, so it sticks to a handful of the most frequent letters — things like ‘E’, ‘N’, ‘I’, ‘A’, ‘R’ and ‘L’ — to build your first words. Every word you see will be made only from this starter set; the rest of the alphabet stays out of play for now. Since there's no typing data yet for these letters, their indicators show up gray.
help.rule1.title: It starts with a handful of letters
help.rule2.body: Once you start typing the generated words, KeyLearn starts logging your performance, and you'll see the indicators shift from red toward green. Red marks a key you're typing slowly, while green marks one you're typing quickly. Your job at this stage is to turn every letter green by picking up speed. Notice that in this example, ‘A’ is called out because it has the slowest typing speed of the bunch, which makes it the target letter. That target letter shows up in every word you're given — worth remembering, because it means you're always drilling the exact key that's currently slowing you down.
help.rule2.title: You get comfortable with those letters
help.rule3.body: Once your speed picks up and every letter has turned green, a new letter — ‘T’ — joins the set, and the words you're given from now on are drawn from this larger pool. ‘T’ becomes the new target letter and appears in every word. As before, since there's no data on it yet, its indicator starts out gray.
help.rule3.title: More letters join the set
help.rule4.body: Now your goal is to turn this newest letter green too, and once you do, another letter gets added and the whole cycle repeats. In practice, don't be surprised if the letters you'd already mastered slip back toward red for a while, as shown here — that's completely normal. Your focus doesn't change: get the current target letter to green so the next one unlocks.
help.rule4.title: You master the newly added letters
help.rule5.body: Stick with it, and eventually every single letter will turn green. That's the main milestone, and you should feel great about reaching it! It doesn't have to be the end, though — keep practicing for as long as you'd like.
help.rule5.title: Rinse and repeat
help.section1:
Type faster, the smart way

What is touch typing?

KeyLearn teaches you touch typing — hitting the right keys from muscle memory alone, with no need to glance down at the keyboard. Mastering it can dramatically boost both your speed and accuracy. Its opposite is hunt-and-peck typing, where you keep your eyes on the keys instead of the screen and rely on just your index fingers.
help.section2:
How the lessons are built

KeyLearn takes a different approach: it leans on statistics and adaptive algorithms to build typing drills tailored to exactly where your skills stand right now. It does this by looping through three steps:

  1. Based on the typing data gathered so far, the algorithm figures out your current skill level and generates a batch of random words built from a letter set it chooses for you.
  2. You type those words, aiming to keep your mistakes to a minimum.
  3. While you type, the algorithm records fresh statistics — including how long each key takes you to hit — and feeds them back into step one to build the next batch of words.

All you have to do at every stage is type the words you're given; KeyLearn handles the rest.
help.section3:
How words are generated

KeyLearn builds random words that still sound natural and readable, following the phonetic patterns of your native language — many of them could pass for real words, and some are. Typing text that reads sensibly is far easier than typing a jumble of random letters, and it also helps you internalize the key combinations you'll hit most often. That second part matters a lot: in English, for instance, the letter ‘W’ almost never follows ‘Z’, so this app will never ask you to type that pairing. Instead, you'll practice far more common sequences like ‘the’, ‘that’, and ‘with’ — before long, you'll be flying through the ‘th’ combo.

Here's how the algorithm picks which letters go into those words.
help.section4: Here's exactly what each indicator color means, laid out in the legend below.
help.section5:
Proper keyboard hand placement

Rest all your fingers on the home row — the row that contains the Caps Lock key. You'll feel small raised bumps on the ‘F’ and ‘J’ keys; line your index fingers up with those. From there, every finger owns a specific group of keys, shown in the illustration below.
help.section6:
Does this app actually work?

Below are a handful of real, anonymized user profiles showing how people's touch typing improved while using KeyLearn. We hope seeing their progress motivates you to keep at it!

m_tour01:
Type Faster With Confidence

KeyLearn teaches you touch typing — typing from muscle memory instead of hunting for keys with your eyes. It can boost both your speed and accuracy by a wide margin. The alternative is hunt-and-peck typing, where you keep glancing down at the keyboard and rely mostly on your index fingers.

This short walkthrough covers how the app works.

Use the left and right arrow keys to move between these slides.
m_tour02:
Here’s what our teaching approach is built on:

No tedious drilling. Unlike many typing tutors, KeyLearn never makes you repeat the same block like ‘jjf jjk jjf jjk’ over and over. That gets tiresome fast and barely helps you learn.

Instead, an algorithm builds lessons that match your current skill level. Each lesson is made of random words drawn from a subset of your alphabet’s letters. The algorithm decides how large that subset is and how often each letter shows up, aiming to give you the most effective learning experience.
m_tour03:
At the start, words are generated from just a handful of the alphabet’s most common letters.

As you type those words, the app tracks a time-to-type measurement for each letter in the subset. That measurement is how your progress gets tracked — the more comfortable you get with a letter, the faster you type it.

Once you’re comfortable with the whole current subset, the algorithm grows it by folding in additional letters.
m_tour04:
Whenever a new letter joins the subset, its frequency gets boosted so it shows up in nearly every generated word of a lesson.

The algorithm also reshuffles letter frequencies on purpose, giving more weight to whichever letters have the slowest time-to-type readings.

In practice, that keeps you typing the letters you’re least comfortable with.
m_tour05: This is the text board, showing the passage you need to type. It refreshes with every new lesson and is built automatically from your current letter subset. Most of these words aren’t real — they’re generated from your language’s phonetic rules so they still sound natural and are easy to pronounce. It’s a bit playful, and it also lets us draw from a far larger pool of words than actually exist.
m_tour06: This is the virtual keyboard, which helps you memorize where each key sits. Use it to locate keys instead of glancing down at your physical keyboard. Your keyboard’s F and J keys have small raised bumps — feel for these to line up your index fingers without looking. Once your index fingers are correctly placed, you’ll be able to find every other key from there.
m_tour07:
This shows your typing speed and how it compares to your average. Higher numbers here are the goal.

Speed is measured in either Words per Minute (WPM) or Characters per Minute (CPM). Since a word is standardized to five characters, 10WPM works out to 50CPM.

You can toggle between WPM and CPM on the Settings page.
m_tour08:
This is your accuracy reading, along with how it compares to your average. As with speed, higher is better here.

Accuracy is the percentage of characters you typed correctly. Repeated mistakes at the same spot only count as a single error.
m_tour09:
This is your score, shown in abstract points, along with how it differs from your average.

It’s calculated from your speed, your error count, and how many letters are currently in your set. The formula rewards fast typing and penalizes mistakes, so typing quickly while making lots of errors won’t earn you a high score.
m_tour10: This trail maps the letters currently used to build your lessons, in the order you unlock them, each one coloured by how confident you are with it:
m_tour11: Hovering a stop on the trail forecasts how many lessons remain before that letter fully unlocks, as shown in the sample chart below. Check back often for a clearer picture of how your learning is progressing.
m_tour12:
This shows details for the letter that’s currently boosted in frequency and appearing in every generated word:

Top typing speed
The fastest you’ve ever typed this particular letter.
Confidence score
A value between zero and one, calculated from your typing speed, showing how well you know this letter. Once confidence reaches one, the letter counts as fully learned.
Learning rate
How your speed on this letter is trending from lesson to lesson.

page.highScores.content:
High Scores

This table ranks the fastest typists from the past few days, sorted from the highest score down. Your typing score factors in your typing speed, how long the text was, how many distinct characters it contained, and how many errors you made. The formula rewards faster speeds, longer passages, and a wider variety of characters, while it penalizes mistakes.
page.highScores.description: See how the fastest typists rank.
page.layouts.content:
Keyboard Layouts

These charts show how efficient each keyboard layout is — in other words, how easy that layout is to type on.

Circle size reflects how often each key is used, and arcs show how often each pair of keys is typed one after another.

Typing is easiest when your most-used keys sit on the home row and your most common key pairs alternate between different fingers and hands. That's why an efficient layout has its biggest circles clustered on the home row, along with arcs spread evenly across the keyboard that run long and horizontal rather than short and diagonal — a sign that fingers and hands are switching off frequently.

setting.keyboardOrder.description: Orders the letters so the home row comes first, followed by the top row, then everything else. The home row is the one with the CapsLock key; the top row is the one with the Tab key. Keeping your fingers on the home row makes typing faster and easier. This works best on optimized layouts such as Dvorak or Colemak. On a Qwerty layout, A is the only home-row vowel, which sharply narrows the choice of words, so the algorithm leans on more pseudo-words than usual.
setting.keyboardOrder.label: Order letters to match the keyboard layout
settings.alphabetSize.description: Manually unlocks the rest of the letters, giving you access to a wider variety of words. Use this sparingly — it’s usually best to let the algorithm unlock letters for you.
settings.benfordsLaw.description: Benford’s law describes a pattern found in many real-world sets of numbers: the first digit tends to be small far more often than not.
settings.benfordsLaw.label: Benford’s law
settings.bottleneckDrill.description: Two keys can each be fast on their own yet drag when you type them back to back — an awkward roll or a same-finger jump. With this on, KeyLearn watches the gaps between your keystrokes, finds the slowest pair among your current keys, and steers the generated words toward it so you smooth out the transition.
settings.capitalLetters.description: Controls how many capital letters show up in the lesson text, so you can practice typing them. Raise this only once every letter is already above your target speed.
settings.customTextLettersOnly.descripti: Strips punctuation marks from the text so it’s simpler to type.
settings.customTextLowercase.description: Converts every character to lowercase so the text is simpler to type.
settings.customTextRandomize.description: Shuffles the words from your text into a random sequence.
settings.dailyGoal.description: Choose how much time you’d like to spend practicing each day. It’s just a gentle reminder, not a limit — you can stop whenever you like.
settings.forgiveErrors.description: When turned on, common slip-ups like a wrong or skipped character are corrected for you automatically.
settings.ghostRace.description: Shows a slim lane above the text with a ghost marker that runs at your fastest pace so far. Stay ahead of it and your marker glows — a friendly race against your past self on every round.
settings.keyboardColors.description: Colors the keyboard by finger zone, so you can see at a glance which finger should press each key.
settings.keyboardPointers.description: Highlights the next key you need to press, so you can find it quickly if you’re still learning where the keys are.
settings.lessonLength.description: Sets how many words appear in each lesson. Longer lessons can help you learn more effectively.
settings.naturalWords.description: Prioritizes real dictionary words, falling back to computer-generated pseudo-words when there aren’t enough real ones available. Real words tend to be easier to type, while pseudo-words offer a far wider variety of letter combinations. With this enabled, you’ll still see plenty of pseudo-words early on, while your letter set is small, but dictionary words are likely to take over almost entirely once you’ve unlocked a few more letters.
settings.punctuation.description: Controls how much basic punctuation shows up in the lesson text, so you can practice typing it. Raise this only once every letter is already above your target speed.
settings.recoverKeys.description: While you’re focused on a new key, your speed on earlier keys will often dip a little. With this option off, a key unlocks as soon as the one you’re focusing on clears the target speed. With it on, every previously unlocked key must also stay above the target speed before a new one unlocks — harder to progress, but it also helps keep you from losing your grip on older keys.
settings.repeatWords.description: Types each word several times in a row. The first pass builds your muscle memory, and each repeat after that should feel a bit easier.
settings.skillDecay.description: Skills rust when they go unused, and this makes the app honest about it. A key you haven't practised in a long while slowly loses a little confidence over real time, gently flagging it for a refresh before it truly slips. Your best-ever result is never wiped — only the current reading softens.
settings.smartConfidence.description: Speed alone can be misleading — a key you hit fast but sloppily isn't really learned. With this on, a Bayesian mastery estimate that watches how cleanly you type is blended into the classic speed reading (speed still leads two-to-one), so a letter only counts as mastered when you're both quick and accurate.
settings.smartPractice.description: These helpers run on top of the core letter-by-letter algorithm during guided practice, quietly steering each session toward whatever pays off most. They're all on by default — switch any of them off if you'd rather keep things classic.
settings.spaceSkipsWords.description: When turned on, pressing space mid-word jumps straight to the start of the next word, skipping whatever's left.
settings.spacedRepetition.description: Skills fade when you stop using them. With this on, KeyLearn keeps an eye on how long it's been since you last drilled each key and quietly brings back the ones that are due — spaced-repetition review woven into your practice. Once every key is unlocked, your sessions turn into targeted refreshers of whatever has gone rusty, so your hard-won speed sticks.
settings.stopCursorOnError.description: When turned on, the cursor won't move forward until you type the correct key. When turned off, mistakes pile up in the text and you'll need to delete them yourself.
settings.targetSpeed.description: Your target speed sets the benchmark behind each letter’s confidence color — the closer you get to it, the greener the letter becomes. In guided mode, a letter unlocks only once you clear this speed threshold. Once every letter is unlocked, raising the target speed re-locks them so you can work toward a faster benchmark. Increase it in small steps, and only once every letter already sits above your current target.
settings.typingAssists.description: These typing assists help you stay in the flow by automatically smoothing over your mistakes.
settings.typingSpeedUnit.description: When measuring typing speed, a word is standardized to five characters or keystrokes in English, counting spaces and punctuation.
